lessons.title: How the browser renders a page
lessons.summary: From bytes to pixels: DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint and compositing, plus what blocks rendering and which changes are cheap.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A browser turns bytes into pixels through a pipeline. Every frame you change something, part of that pipeline runs again. Performance work on the frontend is mostly about two things: getting the **first** run of the pipeline done fast (the critical rendering path) and making **later** runs cheap (touching as few stages as possible).

```text
bytes -> HTML parser -> DOM ----\
                                 +--> Style (computed styles) -> Layout -> Paint -> Composite -> pixels
bytes -> CSS parser  -> CSSOM --/
                 ^
         JS can read and modify both, and can block parsing
```

## Step by step
### 1. Parsing HTML into the DOM
The HTML parser tokenises the byte stream and builds the **DOM**, a tree of nodes. It is incremental: the browser can start working on the top of the document before the bottom arrives. A **preload scanner** runs ahead of the main parser and starts fetching images, stylesheets and scripts it sees in the markup, which is why resources declared in HTML are discovered much earlier than ones injected by JavaScript.

### 2. Parsing CSS into the CSSOM
Stylesheets are parsed into the **CSSOM**. Unlike the DOM it cannot be used partially: a later rule can override an earlier one, so the browser waits for all render-blocking CSS before it renders. That is why CSS is **render-blocking** by default.

### 3. Scripts and the parser
A classic external script (a `script` element with `src`, no attributes) is **parser-blocking**: the parser stops, fetches the script, waits for any pending CSS (the script may read computed styles), executes it, then resumes.

| Attribute | Download | Execution | Order kept |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | blocks parser | immediately | yes |
| `async` | parallel | as soon as downloaded (can interrupt parsing) | no |
| `defer` | parallel | after parsing, before DOMContentLoaded | yes |
| `type="module"` | parallel | deferred by default | yes |

Rule of thumb: app code gets `defer` or `type="module"`; independent third-party scripts such as analytics get `async`.

### 4. Style and the render tree
The browser matches selectors to elements and computes the final value of every property for every element. Elements with `display: none` (and things like `<head>`) are not in the **render tree**; elements with `visibility: hidden` are, because they still take up space.

### 5. Layout (reflow)
Layout computes geometry: the position and size of every box, line breaks, scroll areas. It depends on the viewport, fonts, content and parent sizes, so a change can ripple. Changing one element's width can move its siblings and resize its ancestors.

### 6. Paint
Paint records drawing instructions (text, colours, borders, shadows, images) into display lists for one or more layers, then rasterises them into pixels, usually on raster threads and often on the GPU.

### 7. Composite
The page is split into **layers**. The compositor thread positions and blends those layers to produce the frame. Because it runs off the main thread, it can keep scrolling and some animations smooth even while JavaScript is busy.

## Which changes trigger what
```text
change geometry (width, top, font-size, padding)   -> style -> layout -> paint -> composite
change appearance only (color, background, shadow) -> style ->           paint -> composite
change transform or opacity (on its own layer)     -> style ->                    composite
```

- **Reflow (layout)**: `width`, `height`, `margin`, `padding`, `top/left`, `font-size`, `display`, adding or removing DOM nodes, changing text content, resizing the window.
- **Repaint only**: `color`, `background-color`, `box-shadow`, `outline`, `visibility`.
- **Composite only**: `transform`, `opacity` (and `filter` in many cases) when the element is promoted to its own layer.

Reflow is more expensive than repaint because it is a tree-wide computation and is always followed by paint.

## Forced synchronous layout and thrashing
Browsers batch style changes and lay out once per frame. But if you **read** a layout property (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect()`, `scrollTop`, `getComputedStyle()`) after a **write**, the browser must lay out immediately to give a correct answer.

```ts
// Thrashing: write, read, write, read... one layout per iteration
for (const el of items) {
  el.style.width = `${container.offsetWidth / 2}px`; // read after previous write
}

// Fixed: read once, then write
const half = container.offsetWidth / 2;
for (const el of items) el.style.width = `${half}px`;
```

For animation, do reads and writes inside `requestAnimationFrame`, and prefer `transform` to `top/left`:

```css
/* Animates layout every frame */
.panel.open { left: 0; transition: left 300ms; }

/* Compositor-only: no layout, no paint */
.panel { transform: translateX(-100%); transition: transform 300ms; }
.panel.open { transform: translateX(0); }
```

## Layers: useful, not free
Elements get their own compositor layer for 3D transforms, `will-change: transform`, video, canvas, fixed positioning in some cases, and while a transform or opacity animation runs. Each layer costs GPU memory. Setting `will-change` on hundreds of elements can make a page slower and crash low-memory phones. Add it shortly before an animation and remove it after, or let the browser promote during the animation.

`contain: layout paint` and `content-visibility: auto` let you tell the browser that a subtree is independent, so a change inside it does not invalidate the rest of the page, and off-screen sections can skip rendering entirely.

## The critical rendering path
The critical rendering path is the minimum work needed for the first paint: HTML, the CSS it blocks on, and any parser-blocking scripts. To shorten it:

1. Send fewer critical bytes: inline the small amount of CSS needed above the fold, load the rest non-blocking.
2. Remove parser-blocking scripts from the head: `defer`, `async` or `type="module"`.
3. Cut round trips: `preconnect` to critical third-party origins, `preload` late-discovered critical resources (the LCP image, the main font).
4. Keep the HTML response itself fast: TTFB is the floor for everything else.

## Common mistakes
- Animating `top`, `left`, `width` or `height` instead of `transform`.
- Measuring the DOM inside a loop that also writes styles.
- Putting `will-change` on everything "for performance".
- Believing `async` scripts are always better: they run in arrival order and can interrupt parsing.
- Thinking `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` behave the same for layout.

## In the interview
The classic opener is "what happens from HTML to pixels". Name the stages in order (DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite), then show you know the practical consequences: CSS blocks rendering, scripts block parsing, layout is the expensive step, and transform/opacity skip it. Strong candidates mention the preload scanner, the compositor thread, forced synchronous layout and how they diagnosed a janky animation in the Performance panel (purple Layout blocks, red long-task markers). If asked about frameworks, connect it: a React re-render that produces no DOM change costs JavaScript time but no layout.
keyPoints: Pipeline: parse HTML to DOM, CSS to CSSOM, combine into a render tree, then style, layout, paint and composite
CSS is render-blocking; classic scripts are parser-blocking. Use defer, async or type=module to unblock parsing
Layout (reflow) is the expensive step; changing geometry invalidates layout for the element and often its ancestors and siblings
transform and opacity can be animated on the compositor thread without layout or paint
Reading layout properties right after writing styles forces synchronous layout (layout thrashing); batch reads before writes
interview: Walk me through what the browser does from receiving HTML to painting pixels.
What is the difference between reflow and repaint, and which CSS properties trigger each?
What is layout thrashing and how do you fix it?

check.q: Which change usually skips both layout and paint when the element is on its own compositor layer?
check.why: transform is applied by the compositor to an already painted layer, so layout and paint are skipped. width and font-size need layout; background-color needs paint.

check.q: A classic script tag without async or defer sits in the head. What happens when the parser reaches it?
options: Parsing continues while the script downloads in parallel and runs later
HTML parsing pauses until the script is downloaded and executed
The script is ignored until DOMContentLoaded
check.why: Classic synchronous scripts are parser-blocking because they may call document.write or read the DOM, so the parser must stop, fetch and execute them.

check.q: In a loop you set el.style.height and then read el.offsetHeight for each of 500 elements. What is the problem?
options: Each read forces a synchronous layout because styles were invalidated, causing layout thrashing
Styles are not applied until the next frame, so reads return 0
check.why: Interleaving writes and layout reads forces the browser to recalculate layout on every read. Read everything first, then write, or use requestAnimationFrame.

lessons.title: The event loop, microtasks and rendering
lessons.summary: Call stack, tasks, microtasks, rendering steps, requestAnimationFrame and long tasks, with the output-order puzzles interviewers love.
keyPoints: One loop turn: run one task, drain the whole microtask queue, then maybe render (rAF callbacks, style, layout, paint)
Promise callbacks, await continuations, queueMicrotask and MutationObserver are microtasks; setTimeout, events and message events are tasks
Microtasks can starve rendering: a microtask that queues another microtask blocks the frame forever
Long tasks over 50 ms block input; break work up with scheduler.yield(), setTimeout or a worker
Node has phases (timers, poll, check) plus process.nextTick, which runs before promise microtasks
interview: Explain the event loop, tasks and microtasks.
What is the output order of a snippet mixing setTimeout, Promise.then, async/await and console.log?
How do you keep a long-running computation from freezing the UI?

check.q: What does this print? console.log(1); setTimeout(() => console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)); console.log(4);
check.why: Synchronous code runs first (1, 4). Then the microtask queue drains (3) before the next task, the timeout (2).

check.q: Which of these is scheduled as a microtask?
options: The continuation after await in an async function
check.why: await resumes the async function in a promise reaction job, which is a microtask. The others are tasks.

check.q: A function recursively calls queueMicrotask(itself) forever. What happens to the page?
options: It renders normally because microtasks yield after each callback
It freezes: rendering and input never get a turn because the microtask queue never empties
The browser throws a stack overflow immediately
check.why: The loop drains microtasks until the queue is empty, including newly added ones. An endless chain blocks rendering and tasks, without a stack overflow.

resources.title: MDN: In depth: Microtasks and the JavaScript runtime environment
Jake Archibald: Tasks, microtasks, queues and schedules

lessons.title: JavaScript core concepts interviewers probe
lessons.summary: Scope and closures, hoisting and the TDZ, the four this rules, prototypes, coercion, ESM vs CommonJS, and how memory leaks happen.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Most "tricky JavaScript" questions test whether you have a correct mental model of a few mechanisms: how names are resolved (scope), when bindings exist (hoisting), how `this` is chosen (call site), how properties are looked up (prototypes), and how values are compared (coercion). If you can explain the mechanism, you can predict any snippet.

## Scope and closures
JavaScript is **lexically scoped**: a function can see variables from where it was **written**, not where it is called. A **closure** is a function together with references to those outer variables. The variables stay alive as long as the function is reachable.

```ts
function counter() {
  let count = 0;            // private state
  return {
    inc: () => ++count,
    get: () => count,
  };
}
const c = counter();
c.inc(); c.inc();
c.get(); // 2  -- count lives on after counter() returned
```

Practical uses: private state, factories, memoisation, partial application, debounce/throttle (the timer id lives in the closure), and React hooks (every render's handlers close over that render's props and state).

The classic bug is capturing a **shared** binding:

```ts
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 3 3 3
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 0 1 2
```

`let` in a `for` head creates a new binding per iteration. The React equivalent is a **stale closure**: an effect or interval that captured `count` from the first render keeps seeing the old value.

## Hoisting and the temporal dead zone
Before code runs, the engine creates bindings for declarations in each scope.

| Declaration | Scope | Before the line runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `var` | function | exists, value `undefined` |
| `let` / `const` | block | exists but in the TDZ: access throws `ReferenceError` |
| `class` | block | TDZ |
| `function` declaration | function/block | fully initialised, callable |

```ts
console.log(a); // undefined
var a = 1;

console.log(b); // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
let b = 2;

hello();        // works
function hello() {}
```

The TDZ exists so that `const` really is never observed in two states, and so bugs from using a variable before setup fail loudly.

## How `this` is determined
`this` is not where a function is defined; it is **how it is called**. Check these rules in order:

1. **`new`**: `new Foo()` sets `this` to the newly created object.
2. **Explicit**: `fn.call(obj)`, `fn.apply(obj)`, or a function created by `fn.bind(obj)` (bind wins over later call/apply, but `new` can override it).
3. **Implicit (method call)**: `obj.fn()` sets `this` to `obj`.
4. **Default**: plain `fn()` gives `undefined` in strict mode (modules and classes are always strict) or the global object in sloppy scripts.

**Arrow functions** ignore all four rules: they have no own `this` and use the enclosing scope's.

```ts
const user = {
  name: "Ada",
  hi() { return this.name; },
  later() { setTimeout(function () { console.log(this?.name); }); },  // undefined: default binding
  laterFixed() { setTimeout(() => console.log(this.name)); },          // "Ada": arrow keeps this
};

const hi = user.hi;
hi();              // undefined (strict) -- the method was detached from its object
user.hi.call({ name: "Grace" }); // "Grace"
```

Losing `this` when passing a method as a callback (`button.addEventListener("click", obj.handle)`) is the most common real bug. Fix with an arrow wrapper, `bind`, or a class field arrow function.

## Prototypes and classes
Every object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` link. Property lookup checks the object, then its prototype, then that object's prototype, until `null`.

```ts
class Animal {
  constructor(public name: string) {}
  speak() { return `${this.name} makes a sound`; }
}
class Dog extends Animal {
  speak() { return `${super.speak()} (woof)`; }
}
const d = new Dog("Rex");
// d -> Dog.prototype -> Animal.prototype -> Object.prototype -> null
Object.getPrototypeOf(d) === Dog.prototype; // true
```

Methods live once on the prototype and are shared; instance fields live on each object. Class fields declared as arrow functions are created per instance, which costs memory but binds `this`.

## Equality and coercion
`===` compares without type conversion. `==` converts first using rules few people remember (`"" == 0` is true, `null == 0` is false, `[] == ![]` is true). Use `===` everywhere, with one accepted idiom: `x == null` checks for both `null` and `undefined`.

Other facts worth knowing: `NaN !== NaN` (use `Number.isNaN` or `Object.is`), `Object.is(+0, -0)` is false, objects compare by reference, and `typeof null === "object"` is a historical bug. Falsy values: `false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN`. `??` only falls back on `null`/`undefined`, while `||` falls back on any falsy value, which matters for `count || 10` when `count` is 0.

## ES modules versus CommonJS
| | ES modules | CommonJS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Syntax | `import` / `export` | `require` / `module.exports` |
| Resolution | static, before execution; enables tree shaking | dynamic, at runtime |
| Bindings | live, read-only views of exports | a copy of the exported value at require time |
| Loading | async capable, supports top-level `await` | synchronous |
| `this` at top level | `undefined` | `module.exports` |
| Strict mode | always | opt-in |

Since Node 22 you can `require()` a synchronous ES module (no top-level await), which has eased the interop pain, but dual packages still need care with the `exports` field in `package.json`.

## Garbage collection and memory leaks
Engines use **mark and sweep**: start from roots (globals, the current stack), mark everything reachable, free the rest. Cycles are not a problem. A leak in JavaScript means something you no longer need is **still reachable**. Common causes in SPAs:

- Event listeners on `window` or `document` added on mount and never removed.
- `setInterval` or subscriptions (WebSocket, store) without cleanup.
- Unbounded caches and maps keyed by objects (use `WeakMap` or an LRU limit).
- **Detached DOM nodes**: removed from the page but referenced from a JS variable or closure.
- Closures that capture a large object when they only need one field.

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
  window.addEventListener("resize", onResize);
  return () => window.removeEventListener("resize", onResize); // without this, every mount leaks
}, []);
```

To find leaks: Chrome DevTools Memory panel, take a heap snapshot, perform the action several times (open and close a modal), take another, and compare. Search for "Detached" to find detached DOM trees, then follow the retainers path to the variable holding them.

## Common mistakes
- Saying `let` and `const` are "not hoisted". They are hoisted into the TDZ.
- Explaining `this` as "the object the function belongs to".
- Using arrow functions as object methods that need `this`.
- Believing reference cycles leak in modern engines.

## In the interview
These questions often come as snippets. Read the code, state the rule ("`var` is function-scoped, so all callbacks share one `i`"), then predict. For `this`, list the four rules in priority order plus arrows. For closures, give a real use (debounce, module state, React hooks) and a real bug (stale closure, leaked listener). For leaks, describe the heap snapshot comparison workflow: that is what separates people who have actually fixed one.
keyPoints: A closure is a function plus the variables it captured from its lexical scope; they live as long as the function is reachable
var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined; let, const and class are block-scoped and sit in the temporal dead zone until declared
this is decided by the call site: new, explicit bind/call/apply, method call, or default. Arrow functions take this from the enclosing scope
Classes are syntax over prototypes; property lookup walks the prototype chain
Use === except for the idiom x == null; leaks come from forgotten listeners, timers, caches and detached DOM held by closures
interview: What is a closure? Give a practical use and a bug it can cause.
Explain how `this` is determined in JavaScript.
What are the differences between ES modules and CommonJS?
How do memory leaks happen in a single-page app and how do you find them?

check.q: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); prints what?
check.why: var creates one function-scoped i shared by all callbacks; by the time they run the loop has finished and i is 3. let creates a fresh binding per iteration and prints 0 1 2.

check.q: const obj = { name: 'a', greet: () => this.name }; What does obj.greet() return in an ES module?
options: It throws a TypeError, because this is undefined at module top level
check.why: Arrow functions take this from the enclosing scope. At the top level of an ES module this is undefined, so reading .name throws.

check.q: Which statement about ES modules is true?
options: Imports are live bindings and the module graph is resolved statically before execution
require() and import are interchangeable in every file
ES module exports are copies of values at import time
ES modules run in sloppy mode by default
check.why: ESM imports are static, hoisted and live: if the exporter updates a let binding, importers see the new value. ESM is always strict mode.

lessons.title: Modern CSS: cascade, layout and architecture
lessons.summary: Cascade and specificity, @layer, the box model, flexbox vs grid, stacking contexts, container queries and how teams structure CSS at scale.
keyPoints: The cascade order is origin and importance, then @layer, then specificity, then source order
Specificity is a triple (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements); :where() adds zero, :is() and :not() take their most specific argument
Flexbox lays out one dimension driven by content; grid lays out two dimensions driven by the container
z-index only competes within the same stacking context; transform, opacity below 1, filter and isolation create new ones
Container queries size components by their container, not the viewport, which makes them reusable
interview: How does the CSS cascade decide which rule wins? Explain specificity.
When would you choose grid over flexbox?
Why does z-index: 9999 sometimes not put my element on top?

check.q: Which selector has the highest specificity?
check.why: #menu a is (1,0,1). .nav .item a is (0,2,1), nav ul li a:hover is (0,1,4), and :where() contributes zero so the last is (0,1,1). Any id beats any number of classes.

check.q: A modal has z-index: 1000 but renders under a header with z-index: 10. The modal's parent has transform: translateZ(0). Why?
options: z-index needs position: absolute to work
The parent's transform creates a stacking context, so the modal's z-index only competes inside that parent
The header is position: sticky which always wins
check.why: transform creates a new stacking context. The modal is stacked inside its parent, and the parent as a whole is compared with the header.

check.q: With @layer reset, base, components; declared first, a rule in components and an unlayered rule both target the same element. Which wins (no !important)?
options: The components rule, because it is the last layer
The unlayered rule, because unlayered styles beat all layers
check.why: For normal declarations, unlayered styles take precedence over every named layer, regardless of specificity. Layer order is compared before specificity.

lessons.title: Accessibility that passes audits
lessons.summary: Semantic HTML, accessible names, the rules of ARIA, keyboard and focus management, modal focus traps, live regions, contrast and WCAG 2.2 AA.
lessons.body:
## The core idea Assistive technology (screen readers, switch devices, voice control) does not see your pixels. It reads the **accessibility tree**, which the browser builds from your DOM. Each node in it has a **role** (button, link, heading), a **name** ("Add to cart"), a **state** (expanded, checked, disabled) and sometimes a value. Accessibility work is mostly making that tree correct and making everything operable with a keyboard. Native HTML does both for free; custom widgets have to rebuild them by hand. ## Semantic HTML first ```tsx // Bad: no role, not focusable, no Enter/Space, announced as plain text
Save
// Good: role, focus, keyboard and name for free ``` Structure matters too. Screen reader users navigate by **headings** and **landmarks**, so use one `h1`, a logical heading order, and `header`, `nav`, `main`, `aside`, `footer`. Use `a href` for navigation and `button` for actions. Use real `label` elements tied to inputs, `fieldset` and `legend` for groups of radios, and `table` with `th` for tabular data. ## Accessible names Every interactive element needs a name. The browser computes it, roughly in this priority order: 1. `aria-labelledby` (points at other element ids) 2. `aria-label` 3. Native labelling: `label for`, `alt` on images, `caption`, `legend` 4. Text content (for buttons and links) 5. `title` (last resort, unreliable) ```tsx {/* decorative: empty alt, skipped (next/image) */}

We never share it.

``` You can inspect the computed name in the DevTools Accessibility pane. ## The rules of ARIA ARIA attributes only change the accessibility tree. They add **no behaviour**: `role="button"` does not make a div focusable or respond to Enter. 1. **If a native element does the job, use it instead of ARIA.** 2. Do not change native semantics unless you must (no `

` hacks; wrap instead). 3. All interactive ARIA controls must be keyboard operable. 4. Do not put `role="presentation"` or `aria-hidden="true"` on a focusable element. 5. All interactive elements must have an accessible name. ARIA is genuinely needed for widgets HTML does not have: tabs (`tablist`, `tab`, `tabpanel`), comboboxes and autocomplete, tree views, menus in app-like toolbars, and for **states** like `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-current="page"` and `aria-invalid`. The WebAIM Million survey keeps finding that pages using ARIA have *more* detected errors on average, mostly from ARIA used incorrectly. ## Keyboard and focus - Everything clickable must be reachable with **Tab** and operable with **Enter**/**Space** (and arrows inside composite widgets like tabs and menus, using roving `tabindex`). - Never remove the focus outline without a replacement. Use `:focus-visible` to show it for keyboard users only. - `tabindex="0"` adds an element to the tab order; `tabindex="-1"` makes it focusable by script only; positive values break the natural order and should never be used. - Provide a **skip link** to `main` as the first focusable element. - On client-side route changes, move focus to the new page's `h1` or main region and update the title, or screen reader users hear nothing. ## Building an accessible modal Requirements: focus moves into the dialog when it opens, Tab cycles inside it, the background is inert, **Escape** closes it, and focus returns to the element that opened it. The native element now handles most of this in all evergreen browsers: ```tsx function ConfirmDialog({ open, onClose }: { open: boolean; onClose: () => void }) { const ref = useRef(null); useEffect(() => { const d = ref.current; if (!d) return; if (open && !d.open) d.showModal(); // top layer, background inert, Escape closes if (!open && d.open) d.close(); }, [open]); return (

Delete project?

This cannot be undone.

 ); } ``` `showModal()` places the dialog in the top layer, makes the rest of the page inert, closes on Escape and, in current browsers, returns focus to the previously focused element on close. With a custom div modal you must implement all of it yourself: `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, a focus trap, the `inert` attribute on the rest of the app, and manual focus restoration. ## Live regions Content that changes without a page load (toasts, validation summaries, search result counts, chat messages) must be announced: ```tsx
{message}
{/* waits for a pause */}
{error}
{/* assertive: interrupts */} ``` The region must already be in the DOM before its content changes. Use `alert` sparingly. ## Colour, contrast and WCAG 2.2 AA WCAG 2.2 (a W3C Recommendation since October 2023) at level AA is the common legal and procurement target. Key criteria: | Criterion | Requirement | | --- | --- | | 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum) | 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text | | 1.4.11 Non-text contrast | 3:1 for UI component boundaries, focus indicators, icons that convey meaning | | 1.4.1 Use of colour | Colour is not the only way information is shown (add icons or text to error states) | | 2.4.11 Focus not obscured (new) | A focused element is not entirely hidden by sticky headers or banners | | 2.5.8 Target size (new) | Pointer targets at least 24 by 24 CSS px, or enough spacing | | 3.3.8 Accessible authentication (new) | No cognitive tests such as puzzles for login; allow paste and password managers | | 1.4.10 Reflow | Usable at 320 CSS px wide (400% zoom) without two-dimensional scrolling | Also respect `prefers-reduced-motion` for large animations. ## Testing Automated tools catch roughly a third of WCAG issues (missing names, contrast, invalid ARIA). The rest needs humans. 1. **Automated**: axe DevTools or Lighthouse in the browser; `@axe-core/playwright` or `jest-axe` in CI so regressions fail the build. 2. **Keyboard pass**: unplug the mouse. Can you reach and operate everything? Is focus always visible and in a logical order? 3. **Screen reader pass**: VoiceOver on macOS and iOS, NVDA on Windows, TalkBack on Android. Check names, roles, announcements and reading order. 4. **Zoom and reflow** to 200% and 400%, and test with Windows high contrast (forced colours). Testing Library's `getByRole("button", { name: /save/i })` doubles as an accessibility check: if your test cannot find the element by role and name, neither can a screen reader. ## Common mistakes - `div` and `span` buttons, links without `href`, `outline: none` with no replacement. - `aria-label` on a non-interactive `div` (often ignored) or contradicting the visible text, which breaks voice control. - Placeholder used as the only label. - Modals that do not trap or restore focus; toasts that are never announced. ## In the interview Lead with semantic HTML and the first rule of ARIA, then show you know where ARIA is required (custom widgets, states). For the modal question, list the five behaviours and mention native `dialog` with `showModal()`. For testing, combine automated axe checks in CI with manual keyboard and screen reader passes, and say that automation finds only a fraction of issues. Concrete WCAG numbers (4.5:1, 3:1, 24px targets) signal you have done real audits.
keyPoints: Native elements give you role, name, state and keyboard support for free; the first rule of ARIA is to use them instead of ARIA
Every interactive control needs an accessible name, computed from content, label, aria-labelledby or aria-label
Everything must work with a keyboard, focus must stay visible, and focus must move deliberately when UI opens or closes
Modals: move focus in, trap it, close on Escape, restore focus to the trigger; native dialog with showModal() does most of this
WCAG 2.2 AA: 4.5:1 text contrast (3:1 for large text and UI parts), 24 by 24 px minimum targets, focus not obscured
interview: What is the first rule of ARIA, and when is ARIA actually needed?
How do you build an accessible modal dialog?
How do you test a page for accessibility?

check.q: A clickable div with an onClick handler is reported in an audit. What is the best fix?
options: Replace it with a button element
check.why: A native button is focusable, announced as a button and activates with Enter and Space. role plus tabindex plus key handlers on a div only rebuilds part of that by hand.

check.q: What is the WCAG AA minimum contrast ratio for normal-size body text?
check.why: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (about 24px, or 18.66px bold). 7:1 is the AAA level.

check.q: You show a toast 'Saved' after a form submit. How should screen reader users learn about it?
options: Render it inside a container with role="status" (a polite live region) that already exists in the DOM
Add aria-hidden="true" so it does not interrupt
check.why: A polite live region announces content changes without stealing focus. It must exist before the text is inserted, or many screen readers will not announce it.

lessons.title: Core Web Vitals and performance fixes
lessons.summary: LCP, INP and CLS: what each measures, thresholds, lab versus field data, and the concrete fixes for images, fonts, JavaScript and third parties.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Core Web Vitals are Google's three user-centred metrics for loading, responsiveness and visual stability. They matter for two reasons: they correlate with conversion and engagement, and they are a (small) search ranking signal. More importantly for interviews, they give you a vocabulary to diagnose a slow page methodically instead of guessing.

| Metric | Measures | Good | Poor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **LCP** Largest Contentful Paint | When the largest image or text block in the viewport rendered | at most 2.5 s | over 4 s |
| **INP** Interaction to Next Paint | Latency from a click, tap or key press until the next frame is painted, near the worst across the visit | at most 200 ms | over 500 ms |
| **CLS** Cumulative Layout Shift | How much visible content unexpectedly moves (largest burst of shifts) | at most 0.1 | over 0.25 |

A page "passes" when the **75th percentile** of real page loads is in the good range for all three, measured separately for mobile and desktop.

## Lab versus field
- **Field data (RUM)**: measured on real users' devices. Sources: the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX, a 28-day rolling dataset shown in PageSpeed Insights and Search Console) and your own RUM using the `web-vitals` library. This is the truth, including slow phones and bad networks.
- **Lab data**: Lighthouse, WebPageTest, the DevTools Performance panel. Controlled, repeatable, great for debugging and for CI budgets. But a navigation run has no real interactions, so it reports **Total Blocking Time** as a proxy for INP.

```ts
import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from "web-vitals/attribution";

function send(metric: { name: string; value: number; rating: string; attribution: unknown }) {
  navigator.sendBeacon("/api/vitals", JSON.stringify(metric));
}
onLCP(send);
onINP(send);   // attribution tells you which element and which phase was slow
onCLS(send);
```

## LCP: loading
Break LCP into four parts and fix the biggest:

```text
|-- TTFB --|-- resource load delay --|-- resource load duration --|-- element render delay --|
 server       discovering the image     downloading it              blocked by CSS/JS, hydration
```

Fixes by part:
- **TTFB**: cache HTML at the CDN, stream the response, avoid server waterfalls, static or ISR for content pages.
- **Load delay**: make the LCP image discoverable in the initial HTML (an `img`, not a JS-rendered or CSS background image); add `fetchpriority="high"`; never `loading="lazy"` on the LCP image; `preload` it if it must be late-discovered.
- **Load duration**: modern formats (AVIF, WebP), correct `srcset` and `sizes` so phones do not download desktop images, a CDN with image resizing.
- **Render delay**: remove render-blocking CSS and JS, inline critical CSS, avoid client-only rendering of the hero (server-render it), and avoid hiding content until hydration or A/B test scripts finish.

```tsx
// next/image generates srcset, sizes and modern formats for you
<Image
  src="/hero.jpg"
  sizes="(max-width: 640px) 100vw, 1200px"
  width={1200} height={600}
  priority            // fetchpriority="high", no lazy loading
  alt="Running shoes on a track"
/>
```

In Next.js, `next/image` with the `priority` prop (or `preload` in newer versions) handles most of this.

## INP: responsiveness
Each interaction has three phases:

```text
input delay      -> processing time         -> presentation delay
(main thread       (your event handlers)       (style, layout, paint of
 busy with other                                 the next frame)
 tasks)
```

Debugging: in the field, use `web-vitals/attribution` to find the slow element and phase. In the lab, record the interaction in the Performance panel with CPU throttling and look for long tasks.

Fixes:
- **Input delay**: break up long tasks during load (hydration, third-party scripts); defer non-critical JS.
- **Processing**: do the minimum before the next paint. Update the UI first, then yield, then do the expensive work.
- **Presentation**: avoid huge DOM updates (virtualise long lists), avoid layout thrashing, use `content-visibility: auto` for off-screen sections.

```ts
button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  showSpinner();                         // visible feedback in the next frame
  await yieldToMain();                   // scheduler.yield() or a setTimeout fallback
  runExpensiveFilter();                  // after the browser has painted
});
```

In React, `useTransition` and `useDeferredValue` mark updates as non-urgent so typing stays responsive while a big list re-renders.

## CLS: visual stability
A layout shift happens when a visible element changes position between frames without a recent user input (shifts within 500 ms of an input are excluded). CLS reports the largest **session window** of shifts (bursts up to 5 s with gaps under 1 s).

Causes and fixes:
- **Images and video without dimensions**: always set `width` and `height` or `aspect-ratio` so space is reserved.
- **Ads, embeds and banners injected late**: reserve a fixed-size slot; put consent banners in an overlay rather than pushing content.
- **Web fonts**: swapping from fallback to web font changes text size. Use `font-display: optional` or `swap` with a metric-matched fallback (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`; `next/font` does this automatically), and preload the main font.
- **Animations of layout properties**: animate `transform` instead of `top` or `height`.
- **Content inserted above existing content** after a fetch: use skeletons with the final size.

## Third-party scripts
Tag managers, chat widgets, A/B testing and ads are a leading cause of poor INP and LCP. Audit them with the DevTools third-party badges, load with `async` or after interaction, use facades (show a static image of the chat or video player until clicked), and consider moving them off the main thread with Partytown where compatible. A/B testing scripts that hide the page until they run directly delay LCP.

## Performance budgets
Turn targets into checks that fail CI:
- Lighthouse CI assertions (for example LCP under 2.5 s on a throttled profile, TBT under 200 ms, CLS under 0.1).
- Bundle size limits per route (`size-limit` or the build output), for example 170 KB of compressed JS for the initial route.
- RUM dashboards that alert when the p75 regresses after a deploy.

## Common mistakes
- Optimising the Lighthouse score while field data is what matters.
- Lazy-loading the hero image, or preloading ten resources so none is actually prioritised.
- Measuring INP only on a fast laptop.
- Thinking CLS only happens during load; it is measured for the page's whole life, including SPA navigations.

## In the interview
State the three metrics, what they measure and the thresholds at the 75th percentile, and that INP replaced FID in 2024. For "fix a 4-second LCP", do not list random tips: first identify the LCP element, break the time into its four parts, then fix the biggest one. For INP, name the three phases and show you know about yielding and transitions. Mention lab versus field and how you would set budgets in CI and watch RUM after deploys.
keyPoints: Good thresholds at the 75th percentile of real users: LCP at most 2.5 s, INP at most 200 ms, CLS at most 0.1
INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in March 2024; it measures the slowest interactions across the whole visit, not just the first input delay
Field data (CrUX, RUM with the web-vitals library) is what counts; lab tools (Lighthouse) are for debugging and regression checks
Break LCP into TTFB, resource load delay, load duration and render delay, then fix the largest part
CLS comes from unsized media, late-injected content and web font swaps; reserve space and animate with transform
interview: What are the Core Web Vitals and what does each one measure?
How would you improve a page with a 4-second LCP?
What is INP and how do you debug a poor INP score?

check.q: Which metric replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024?
check.why: INP replaced FID. It covers the full latency (input delay, processing and presentation) of interactions throughout the page's life.

check.q: The LCP element is a hero image set as a CSS background in a stylesheet loaded by JavaScript. What is the biggest problem?
options: Background images cannot be the LCP element
The image is discovered late, so resource load delay is large; use an img in the HTML with fetchpriority="high" or preload it
CSS backgrounds are always decoded on the main thread
check.why: The preload scanner cannot see an image referenced from JS-injected CSS, so the download starts late. Putting it in HTML or preloading it removes that delay.

check.q: Lighthouse shows a great score but CrUX reports poor INP. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Lighthouse does not measure INP; real users interact on slower devices with more state, triggering long tasks the lab run never exercises
CrUX data is always wrong for single-page apps
INP only counts the first click, which Lighthouse simulates
check.why: A Lighthouse navigation run has no user interactions; TBT is only a proxy. Field INP comes from real clicks and taps on real devices.

lessons.title: TypeScript patterns for UI code
lessons.summary: Typing props and events, generic components and hooks, discriminated unions for state, narrowing, utility types, satisfies and validating API data with zod.
keyPoints: Model UI state as a discriminated union so impossible states (loading with data and an error) cannot be represented
Narrowing (typeof, in, equality on a tag, type predicates) plus a never check makes switches exhaustive
Generics let one component or hook keep the caller's types, for example a List<T> or useFetch<T>
satisfies checks a value against a type without widening it, so you keep literal types and autocomplete
Types vanish at runtime: validate network data with zod at the boundary and infer the type from the schema; prefer unknown to any
interview: How would you model loading, success and error state in TypeScript?
How do you write a generic React component or hook?
What is the difference between `unknown`, `any` and `never`?

check.q: type State = { status: 'idle' } | { status: 'ok'; data: User } | { status: 'error'; error: string }. After if (s.status === 'ok'), what is the type of s?
check.why: Checking the discriminant narrows the union to the matching member, so s.data is available and typed as User.

check.q: What is the main advantage of `const routes = { home: '/' } satisfies Record<string, string>` over annotating `const routes: Record<string, string>`?
options: It validates the value at runtime
It checks the shape but keeps the inferred type, so routes.home is known to exist and routes.typo is an error
check.why: An annotation widens the type to Record<string, string>, losing the specific keys. satisfies checks compatibility and keeps the narrower inferred type.

check.q: You receive JSON from fetch. Which approach actually protects you from a backend shape change?
options: Parse it with a zod schema and use the inferred type
Declare the response type in a .d.ts file
check.why: Type assertions and declarations do nothing at runtime. A schema parse checks the actual data and fails at the boundary with a clear error.

lessons.title: Browser networking and caching
lessons.summary: Cache-Control, ETags and immutable assets, CDNs, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, resource hints, service workers, browser storage options and CORS.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
The fastest request is the one you never make; the second fastest is one answered from a nearby cache. Browser networking for a frontend engineer comes down to: cache aggressively what never changes, revalidate cheaply what might, cut connection setup time, tell the browser what is important, and know which storage to use for what.

## HTTP caching
The browser's HTTP cache and every CDN in between follow the `Cache-Control` header.

| Directive | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `max-age=N` | Fresh for N seconds; use without asking the server |
| `s-maxage=N` | Same, but for shared caches (CDN) only |
| `no-cache` | May store, but must revalidate before each use |
| `no-store` | Never store (sensitive data) |
| `private` / `public` | Only the browser may cache, or shared caches too |
| `immutable` | Will never change during its freshness; do not revalidate even on reload |
| `stale-while-revalidate=N` | Serve stale for up to N seconds while refetching in the background |

**Revalidation**: the server sends a validator, `ETag: "abc123"` (or `Last-Modified`). When the cached copy is stale, the browser sends `If-None-Match: "abc123"`; if nothing changed, the server answers `304 Not Modified` with no body.

```text
first visit:   GET /app.3f9a1c.js  -> 200, Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
next visits:   served from disk cache, no request at all

first visit:   GET /index.html     -> 200, Cache-Control: no-cache, ETag: "v42"
next visits:   GET /index.html, If-None-Match: "v42" -> 304 (tiny) or 200 with new HTML
```

### The standard SPA / Next.js recipe
- **Fingerprinted assets** (`app.3f9a1c.js`, hashed CSS, images): `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. A new deploy produces new file names, so stale content is impossible.
- **HTML** (the file that references the hashes): `no-cache`, or a short `s-maxage` with `stale-while-revalidate` at the CDN. Never cache HTML for a long time in the browser, or users keep loading old bundles that may no longer exist.
- **API responses**: usually `private, no-cache` or `no-store` for personal data; public data can use `s-maxage` with `stale-while-revalidate`.

## CDNs
A CDN caches responses at edge locations close to users, cutting round-trip time and offloading the origin. Key concepts: the **cache key** (URL plus selected headers and cookies; a cookie in the key can kill the hit rate), `Vary` (cache a separate copy per `Accept-Encoding` or `Accept-Language`), **purging** or tag-based invalidation after content changes, and edge compression with Brotli.

## HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
- **HTTP/1.1**: one request at a time per connection; browsers open about 6 connections per origin. This is why domain sharding, sprites and concatenation existed.
- **HTTP/2**: one TCP connection, many concurrent streams (multiplexing), compressed headers (HPACK). Sharding becomes harmful. But one lost TCP packet stalls every stream (TCP head-of-line blocking).
- **HTTP/3**: runs over **QUIC** on UDP. Streams are independent, so a lost packet only stalls its own stream. TLS 1.3 is built in, setup is faster (one round trip, or zero for resumed connections), and connections survive network changes such as Wi-Fi to mobile. It helps most on lossy mobile networks.

HTTP/2 server push has been removed from Chrome; use `preload` and `103 Early Hints` instead.

## Resource hints
```html
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://cdn.example.com" crossorigin />
<link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://analytics.example.com" />
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin />
<link rel="preload" href="/hero.avif" as="image" fetchpriority="high" />
<link rel="prefetch" href="/checkout.js" />
<link rel="modulepreload" href="/assets/router.js" />
```

- **preconnect**: do DNS, TCP and TLS now for an origin you will use soon. Limit to two or three critical origins; unused connections waste CPU.
- **dns-prefetch**: only the DNS lookup; cheap fallback for less critical origins.
- **preload**: fetch a resource the **current page** definitely needs but discovers late (fonts in CSS, an LCP background image, a late script). High priority. Unused preloads produce console warnings and steal bandwidth.
- **prefetch**: fetch at low priority something the **next navigation** will likely need. Next.js `Link` prefetches routes in the viewport.
- **modulepreload**: preload an ES module and its parsing.
- The **Speculation Rules API** (Chromium) can prefetch or fully prerender likely next pages from a JSON rule set.

## Service workers and offline
A service worker is a script that sits between your page and the network for its scope. It can intercept `fetch` events and answer from a programmable cache, which enables offline support and instant repeat loads.

```ts
// sw.ts (simplified)
const VERSION = "v3";
self.addEventListener("install", (e: ExtendableEvent) => {
  e.waitUntil(caches.open(VERSION).then((c) => c.addAll(["/", "/offline", "/app.css"])));
});
self.addEventListener("fetch", (e: FetchEvent) => {
  if (e.request.mode === "navigate") {
    // network first for HTML, offline page as fallback
    e.respondWith(fetch(e.request).catch(() => caches.match("/offline") as Promise<Response>));
  }
});
```

Common strategies: **cache first** for fingerprinted assets, **network first** for HTML and API data that must be fresh, **stale-while-revalidate** for things like avatars. The lifecycle (install, waiting, activate) means a new worker waits until all tabs using the old one close, unless you call `skipWaiting()`, which can mix old pages with new assets. Workbox wraps these patterns. Service workers require HTTPS (or localhost).

## Browser storage
| | Cookies | localStorage | sessionStorage | IndexedDB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Size | about 4 KB each | about 5 MB per origin | about 5 MB, per tab | large (a share of disk) |
| Sent to server | with every matching request | no | no | no |
| API | header / `document.cookie` | synchronous strings | synchronous strings | async, structured data, indexes, transactions |
| Lifetime | until expiry | until cleared | until the tab closes | until cleared or evicted |
| Workers | no | no | no | yes |
| JS-readable | not if `HttpOnly` | yes | yes | yes |

Guidance: session tokens belong in `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` cookies so injected scripts cannot read them. localStorage is for small, non-sensitive preferences; it blocks the main thread on large values. IndexedDB (usually through a wrapper like `idb` or Dexie) is for offline data, drafts and caches. Call `navigator.storage.persist()` to reduce the risk of eviction, especially on Safari, which may clear script-written storage for sites not visited in seven days.

## CORS basics
The **same-origin policy** stops a page from reading responses from another origin (scheme, host and port). CORS lets the server opt in with headers.

- **Simple requests** (GET, HEAD or POST with a form-type content type and no custom headers) are sent directly; the browser blocks reading the response unless `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` matches.
- Anything else (PUT, DELETE, `application/json`, an `Authorization` header) triggers a **preflight** `OPTIONS` request first. The server must reply with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Methods` and `-Headers`; `Access-Control-Max-Age` caches the preflight.
- With credentials (`fetch(url, { credentials: "include" })`) the server must echo the exact origin (not `*`) and send `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

CORS is enforced by the browser to protect users. It is not server security: curl ignores it. It also does not stop CSRF on simple requests, which is what `SameSite` cookies and CSRF tokens are for.

## Common mistakes
- Long `max-age` on `index.html`, leaving users on old builds.
- Using `no-cache` when you meant `no-store` (or the reverse) for sensitive pages.
- Preloading fonts without `crossorigin`, so they download twice.
- Storing JWTs in localStorage, where any XSS can steal them.
- Fixing CORS errors by proxying everything or by `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials, which browsers reject anyway.

## In the interview
For caching, give the two-tier recipe (immutable hashed assets, revalidated HTML) and explain ETag and 304. For resource hints, define each by "this page now" versus "next page" versus "just the connection". For storage, compare size, sync versus async, server visibility and XSS exposure, and say where you would put a session token. For CORS, say who enforces it, when a preflight happens and what headers fix it.
keyPoints: Fingerprinted static assets get Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable; HTML gets no-cache or a short max-age so deploys show up
no-cache means revalidate before use (ETag / If-None-Match gives a cheap 304); no-store means never store
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one TCP connection; HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP and removes TCP head-of-line blocking
preconnect warms a connection, preload fetches a resource needed for this page now, prefetch fetches one likely needed for the next navigation
Cookies are sent with every request and can be HttpOnly; localStorage is synchronous and small; IndexedDB is async, large and works in workers
interview: How do you set up HTTP caching for a single-page app's HTML and static assets?
What is the difference between preload, prefetch and preconnect?
Compare cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB.
What is CORS and why does a preflight request happen?

check.q: What does Cache-Control: no-cache mean?
options: The response must never be stored
The response may be stored but must be revalidated with the server before each use
The response expires after one hour
Only the CDN may cache it
check.why: no-cache allows storing but requires revalidation (often a cheap 304 via ETag). no-store is the directive that forbids storing.

check.q: Which resource hint fits the main web font that the CSS references and the current page needs immediately?
check.why: preload fetches a resource the current page definitely needs at high priority. Fonts require the crossorigin attribute even on the same origin, or the preload is wasted.

check.q: A fetch from app.example.com to api.example.com with Content-Type: application/json fails before the POST is sent. Why?
options: Browsers block all cross-origin POST requests
JSON content type makes it a non-simple request, so the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight, and the API did not answer it with the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers
check.why: Different subdomains are different origins. Non-simple requests need a successful preflight that allows the origin, method and headers before the real request is sent.

projects.title: High-performance, accessible e-commerce storefront
projects.summary: A product listing, filterable catalogue, product page, cart and checkout UI that stays in the green on all Core Web Vitals on a mid-range phone and passes WCAG 2.2 AA, with budgets enforced in CI.
projects.why: Every e-commerce company ties speed to revenue, and most storefronts fail Core Web Vitals on mobile. A project that shows measured p75 LCP, INP and CLS, performance budgets that fail the build, and audited accessibility proves you can ship fast and inclusive UI, not just make it look right. It gives you real numbers to talk about in every frontend interview.
projects.architecture:
```text
Browser
  |  HTML streamed (RSC)        static assets: hashed, immutable, CDN
  v
Next.js on Vercel / CDN
  +-- /                 static + ISR (revalidate on product change)
  +-- /c/[category]     server-rendered list, filters in searchParams
  +-- /p/[slug]         static product page, next/image, JSON-LD
  +-- /cart, /checkout  client islands (cart store), server actions
  +-- /api/vitals       RUM beacon endpoint -> storage -> p75 dashboard
  |
Catalogue source (JSON / headless CMS / Postgres) validated with zod
CI: typecheck -> unit -> Playwright + axe -> Lighthouse CI budgets -> deploy
```
Key decisions:
- Server Components for catalogue pages so product HTML ships without client JS; only filters, cart and checkout hydrate.
- Filter state lives in the URL (`searchParams`) so it is shareable, back-button friendly and server-renderable.
- The LCP image on each template is known and prioritised; everything below the fold is lazy.
- Budgets are numbers in a config file that fail CI, not a goal in a README.

Checkable: every route renders server-side with JavaScript disabled

milestones.title: Product listing with URL-driven filters

Wrap the results update in useTransition so filter clicks stay responsive while the list re-renders
Paginate or virtualise so the DOM stays under about 1500 nodes
Checkable: a filtered URL pasted into a new tab shows the same results

milestones.title: Images, fonts and LCP

next/font with a metric-matched fallback; no layout shift when the font swaps
Checkable: Lighthouse on a throttled mobile profile shows LCP under 2.5 s and CLS under 0.1 on home, category and product pages

milestones.title: Cart and checkout UI
details: Cart in a small client store persisted to localStorage, with an optimistic add-to-cart that rolls back on failure
Checkout form with labelled inputs, autocomplete attributes, inline errors linked by aria-describedby and an error summary that receives focus on submit
Server Action validates the order with the same zod schema as the client
Checkable: complete a purchase using only the keyboard

milestones.title: Accessibility audit

Playwright tests run axe-core on every route and fail on any serious or critical violation

web-vitals with attribution beacons to /api/vitals; a dashboard page shows p75 LCP, INP and CLS by route and device
Checkable: a pull request that adds a 200 KB library to the product page fails CI

A short case study: the worst INP interaction you found, its attribution data and the fix

Speculation Rules to prerender the product page on hover
Edge-cached personalised price formatting by locale without breaking the CDN cache
Image CDN with AVIF and art-directed crops
Offline cart with a service worker
resume: Built a Next.js storefront with [X] products that holds p75 LCP at [Y] s, INP at [Z] ms and CLS at [N] on mid-range Android devices, measured with real-user monitoring
Cut product-page JavaScript by [X]% by moving catalogue rendering to React Server Components and hydrating only the cart and filters
Enforced performance budgets in CI with Lighthouse CI, blocking [X] regressions before release
Reached WCAG 2.2 AA with zero serious axe violations across [X] routes, verified with keyboard and screen reader testing
talking: How I identified the LCP element per template and which of its four sub-parts dominated
Why filter state lives in the URL and how useTransition keeps filtering under 200 ms INP
Lab versus field: where Lighthouse and RUM disagreed and why
What the axe tests caught and what only manual screen reader testing found
The cache headers for HTML, hashed assets and product images, and how ISR invalidates product pages
features: Server-rendered home, category and product pages that load fast on a throttled phone
Filterable, sortable product grid with shareable URLs and instant feedback
Product page with image gallery, variant picker and structured data
Accessible multi-step checkout form with inline validation
Fully keyboard and screen reader operable, including the filter drawer
Live Web Vitals dashboard from real visits, by route

deepDives.title: Getting LCP under 2.5 s on every template
deepDives.body:
Start by finding the LCP element per template (DevTools Performance panel or `onLCP` attribution). On the home page it is usually the hero image, on category pages the first product image, on product pages the main gallery image.

Then break the time down:

```text
TTFB | load delay | load duration | render delay
```

- **TTFB**: catalogue pages are static or ISR, so HTML comes from the CDN in tens of milliseconds. Avoid per-request data fetching on these routes; personalised bits (cart count) render as a small client island.
- **Load delay**: the image must be in the server HTML, not behind a client fetch, with `priority` on `next/image` so it gets `fetchpriority="high"` and no lazy loading. Only one or two images per page should be prioritised, or the hint means nothing.
- **Load duration**: correct `sizes` matters more than format. Without it, a phone may download the 1200 px version. Serve AVIF/WebP through the image optimiser.
- **Render delay**: keep render-blocking CSS small (Tailwind output is usually a few KB), no client-side A/B scripts that hide the page, and do not wait for hydration to show the hero.

Verify with a throttled Lighthouse run in CI and confirm with p75 field data, which is what actually counts.

deepDives.title: Keeping filter interactions under 200 ms INP
Budgets that fail the build
Accessible checkout and filter drawer
deepDives.body:
Checkout is where accessibility failures cost money directly.

- Every input has a visible `label`, the right `type` and `autocomplete` (`email`, `postal-code`, `cc-number`) so browsers and password managers can fill it.
- Errors are shown inline, linked with `aria-describedby`, marked with `aria-invalid`, and not shown by colour alone. On submit with errors, focus moves to an error summary listing links to each invalid field.
- The filter drawer on mobile is a native `dialog` opened with `showModal()`, so focus is trapped, the page behind is inert and Escape closes it. Closing returns focus to the Filters button.
- The results count lives in a `role="status"` region so screen reader users hear "24 products" after filtering.
- Touch targets are at least 24 by 24 px (WCAG 2.2 target size), and the sticky header never hides the focused element (focus not obscured).

Playwright with `@axe-core/playwright` fails CI on serious violations, but the README also documents a manual VoiceOver pass, because automated tools catch only a fraction of real issues.

projects.title: Offline-first PWA notes app
projects.summary: A notes app that works fully offline: every edit is saved locally first, synced in the background when the network returns, conflicts are detected and resolved, and the app installs to the home screen.
projects.why: Offline-first forces you to understand the parts of the browser most candidates only know by name: service worker lifecycle, cache strategies, IndexedDB transactions, background sync and storage eviction. Conflict handling is a genuine distributed-systems problem on the client. It is a strong talking point for frontend system design rounds (Google Docs, Notion, field-worker apps).
projects.architecture:
```text
UI (React)
  | reads and writes only local data (instant)
  v
Local store: IndexedDB
  notes(id, title, body, updatedAt, version, deleted)
  outbox(opId, noteId, op, baseVersion, createdAt)
  |
  v
Sync engine (in page, or triggered by the service worker 'sync' event)
  push outbox -> POST /sync/push   (server checks baseVersion)
  pull changes -> GET /sync/pull?since=cursor
  |
Service worker: precache app shell (cache first), network first for API,
                offline fallback, Background Sync where supported
  |
Server: notes table with version per note + change log with cursor
```
Key decisions:
- Local-first: the UI never waits on the network; the server is a sync peer, not the source of every read.
- An outbox of operations instead of "sync the whole note list" keeps sync idempotent and resumable.
- Per-note version numbers detect conflicts; resolution is explicit (keep both or merge) rather than silent last-write-wins.
- Background Sync is a progressive enhancement: Chromium only, so the app also syncs on `online` events and on focus.

deepDives.title: Service worker caching and the update flow
deepDives.body:
The app shell (HTML, hashed JS and CSS, icons) is precached at install with Workbox, which generates a manifest of file hashes at build time. Strategies by request type:

| Request | Strategy | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hashed JS/CSS | cache first | file names change on deploy |
| Navigations | app shell from cache, then the SPA routes | instant offline start |
| `/sync/*` API | network only (the outbox handles offline) | never serve stale sync data |
| Avatars, images | stale-while-revalidate | fast, eventually fresh |

The tricky part is updates. A new service worker installs but **waits** while any tab still uses the old one. Calling `skipWaiting()` immediately can activate new code under a page that loaded old chunks, causing missing-chunk errors. Instead, the page listens for a waiting worker, shows "New version available", and on click posts a message that triggers `skipWaiting()`, then reloads on `controllerchange`. This gives a predictable, user-controlled update.

deepDives.title: Outbox pattern and idempotent sync
Conflict detection: versions, last-write-wins and CRDTs
deepDives.body:
Each note has a server version number. A push says "I edited version 7". If the server is at 7, it applies the change and returns 8. If it is already at 8 (another device synced first), it rejects the op and returns the server copy.

Options for resolution:
- **Last-write-wins** by timestamp: simple, but silently loses one user's edits and depends on clocks. Acceptable for fields like "pinned", not for body text.
- **Surface the conflict**: show both versions and let the user keep one or both. This project does this for note bodies: it is honest and easy to reason about.
- **CRDTs** (Yjs, Automerge): every edit is an operation that merges automatically and converges on all devices, with character-level merging. Best UX for collaborative text, at the cost of a library, larger stored state and a different server model. Listed as a stretch goal.

In the interview, the point is not that one is right: it is choosing per field based on how bad a lost write is.

deepDives.title: Background Sync, storage limits and eviction
deepDives.body:
The Background Sync API lets the page register a tag (`registration.sync.register("flush-outbox")`); the browser fires a `sync` event in the service worker when connectivity returns, even if the tab was closed. It is supported in Chromium browsers only, so the app treats it as an enhancement and also syncs on `online`, `visibilitychange` and app start.

Storage is not guaranteed. Browsers can evict origin data under storage pressure, and Safari may delete script-writable storage for sites the user has not interacted with in seven days (installed home screen web apps are treated differently). Mitigations:
- Call `navigator.storage.persist()` at a meaningful moment and show the result.
- Show `navigator.storage.estimate()` usage in settings.
- Keep the server as a durable copy: the outbox draining is what makes local data safe.
